summary: **Verification, not self-critique, is what helps.** Over 45 held-out configurations and two repeats, verifier-grounded reflection (A5) was exactly right on 18 configurations where single-agent agentic RAG (A3) was wrong, and never the reverse (exact McNemar p < 0.001). A5 also beat LLM-only reflection (A4, the design of the closest published work) 15 to 2 (p = 0.002). A4 itself did not beat A3 at the 5% level (5 vs 0, p = 0.06).

**The deterministic verifier carries the gain; the LLM critic adds little.** The verifier alone (A6) beat A3 15 to 0 (p < 0.001), and A5 vs A6 was not resolved (3 vs 0, p = 0.25), with A6 using 30% fewer tokens and about a third of the time. This matches hypothesis H3 of the proposal.

**A cross-family critic did not help.** With Llama-3.1-8B as critic (A5x), only 5 of 364 critic claims (1.4%) passed the evidence checks, against 103 of 407 (25%) for the Qwen critic, and A5x behaved like the verifier-only arm.
**Reflection mostly corrects rather than damages.** Across both repeats A5 turned 179 parameter verdicts from wrong to right and 15 from right to wrong; A4 turned 70 right and 40 wrong.

**A small local model over-flags.** Qwen2.5-7B without verification reported about six false violations per true one (precision 0.15). Grounded verification raised precision to 0.25-0.26 and more than doubled citation correctness (8% to 20%), at a cost in recall (0.94 to 0.64-0.68).

**Against the rule scanner:** A0 has the best F1 overall (0.41 vs 0.36-0.37) because it never misses a literal violation, but on exact correctness of the whole file A5 beat A0 15 to 3 (p = 0.008): A0 cannot reason about deployment profiles and never solved a decoy or a context-dependent file.

**Formal repair fixes what the LLM fixes badly.** From the same confirmed findings, SMT minimal repair (A7) raised fix correctness from 21% to 38% and cut unnecessary changes on compliant files from 73% to 29%.

**In the network, wrong fixes cost more than missed findings.** In the closed-loop twin (3 seeds, 6 h each), arms that push LLM-written fixes (A3, A4) left gNBs non-compliant for longer than no agent at all (52 vs 40 site-hours). A7 cut non-compliant site-hours to 25 and users displaced by fixes by 72% compared with A5 (892 vs 3193).

**Provenance checking blocks knowledge-base poisoning, and fails closed.** With a tampered clause in the corpus, A3 and A4 each confirmed 3 findings citing the tampered text; A5 confirmed none, but also dropped a genuine finding that relied on the same clause.

**LLM verdicts are not stable run to run.** The same configuration received the same verdict in both repeats for 82% of files with A3, but only 38% with A5 and 16% with A4; meaning-preserving rewrites changed verdicts on 17-75% of files. A prompt injection hidden in a configuration comment had no effect on detection.
Absolute accuracy is low (best exact match 27%) because of the small local model and the deliberately hard dataset; the evidence is in the paired differences, not the absolute levels.
e1: Precision limits every LLM arm: A1-A3 produce about 130 false violations against 23-24 true ones per repeat, mostly on drb_integrity and the algorithm lists. Retrieval (A2) and query generation (A3) did not change this with a 7B model (A3 vs A1 and A3 vs A2: no configuration differs).

The verifier's C4 applicability check removed most false positives. 78-84% of A5/A6 runs ended with at least one finding that could not be verified within three rounds and was dropped (escalation). The revision step rarely changed the model's answer, so the gain comes from filtering by checkable evidence rather than from the model learning from feedback.
Decoys and context pairs separate the arms: A0-A3 solved none, A5 solved 25-38% of decoys and 14% of context pairs. Vendor-default files (OAI sample values) were solved by no arm.

A5x latency is not comparable with the other arms: its Qwen assessor calls were served from the cache filled by A5, so only the Llama critic calls were timed. A7's quality columns differ from A5 only in the fix; its latency is A5's plus a few milliseconds of SMT solving.
e2: The injected comment asked the auditor to report the file as compliant. Across 12 non-trivial files no arm missed more violations on the injected variant than on the original (A3: 6 true positives in both; A5: 5 vs 4), so Qwen2.5-7B did not follow the instruction in this test.

Robustness to harmless rewrites differs: the rule scanner is fully deterministic (100% unchanged), A3 kept its verdict on 67-83% of variants and A5 on only 25-75%, because A5's final answer depends on which marginal findings survive verification. Accuracy on the variants was unchanged for every arm (A5 25%, A3 0%, A0 8%).
Practical consequence: a deployment should run the LLM assessor more than once, or treat verdict disagreement as a signal for escalation, rather than act on a single run.
e3: Five poisoned clauses were added: four fake identifiers and one tampered copy of OSB-1 with the same identifier. Poisoned text was retrieved in 4 of 12 runs per arm.

A3 and A4 used the tampered OSB-1 sentence as evidence in 3 confirmed findings each. A5 used it in none: every citation to that chunk failed the hash check against the trusted manifest. Because the tampered chunk replaced the genuine OSB-1, A5 also lost the true ciphering finding on cfg-024; the check cannot tell which citation was meant to be legitimate, so it fails closed.
The remaining verdict changes for A5 under poisoning come from different retrieved context changing the model's output, not from poisoned citations being accepted.
e4: Every arm saw the same mobility, traffic, config drift and attacks within a seed (common random numbers, verified), so differences come from the agent. Values are means over seeds 11-13; per-seed values are in results/e4_twin.json.

Under the operator-hardened profile used here, the literal rule scanner (A0) minimised exposure (6 unciphered active UE-hours vs 311 with no agent) because almost every insecure literal value is also a violation in that profile. Its cost is about 20 unnecessary fix pushes per 6 hours on compliant gNBs.
Verifier-grounded arms reduced successful RRC injection attacks by about 40% compared with A3 (1399 vs 2313) but, with lower recall, left more null-ciphered traffic than A3 (149 vs 96 UE-hours).

Fix quality dominates network outcomes: A3 and A4 increased non-compliant site-hours above the no-agent baseline, while A7, using the same findings as A5 but SMT repair, achieved the lowest non-compliance of any LLM arm with 10 pushes and almost no unnecessary ones.

Remediation timing inside the twin: the maintenance-window policy pushed almost nothing in a 16:00-22:00 run, so its exposure matched no agent; the RL scheduler matched immediate remediation on exposure with 8% fewer users displaced (2950 vs 3193). Over a 6-hour evening window the scheduling effect is small; E6 shows it over full 24-hour cycles.
e5: User-plane integrity protection costs 0.29 percentage points of total goodput and raises VoIP header overhead from 6.5% to 9.9% (4-byte MAC-I on small packets), with 0.05 ms added latency. In this model the performance argument for leaving UP integrity off is weak; the cost concentrates on small-packet traffic.
e6: Over 200 paired 24-hour episodes the learned PPO scheduler beat the best hand-written rule (severity threshold) by 11.5 reward units (95% CI 8.3-14.9; better in 74% of episodes), mainly by deferring low-severity fixes to off-peak hours while fixing high-severity issues immediately. A pure maintenance-window policy is unacceptable when severe violations appear (exposure two orders of magnitude higher).
ns3: The twin's median SINR (3.9 dB) lies within 0.7-1.7 dB of ns-3 5G-LENA on the same layout, which supports its use for relative comparisons. The tails differ: ns-3's beamforming arrays reach higher SINR, and ns-3 shows a low-SINR tail of unresolved origin. Absolute radio KPIs from the twin are therefore indicative only.
